extracted.intended_audience: college/university students writing academic essays, lab reports, and research papers (and instructors revising student writing)
extracted.subtask_short: avoiding passive voice in academic writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying, evaluating, and revising passive-voice constructions in academic writing (humanities and sciences), including when passive is acceptable and when active voice improves clarity. Covers identification rules, evaluation questions, revision techniques, and discipline-specific exceptions (e.g., lab reports).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: passive construction (identification formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: A passive construction occurs when you make the object of an action into the subject of a sentence — the performer of the action is not the grammatical subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sure-fire formula for identifying the passive voice: form of 'to be' + past participle = passive voice. Examples: 'The metropolis has been scorched by the dragon’s fiery breath.' 'The fish was caught by the seagull.' Look for a form of 'to be' (is, are, was, were, has been, have been, had been, will be, being, etc.) followed by a past participle (usually ending in -ed, with exceptions like 'paid' or 'driven'). If the actor appears, it will often be in a 'by...' phrase at the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myth: passive voice is a grammatical error
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of the passive voice is not a grammatical error; it is a stylistic issue related to clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat passive as inherently wrong. It may prevent a reader from understanding what you mean, but it does not constitute a grammar mistake. Evaluate its effect on clarity rather than assuming it is incorrect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myth: any use of 'to be' equals passive
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every sentence that contains a form of 'to be' is passive; 'be' can describe a state rather than indicate a passive action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that 'be' can be the main verb describing a state (e.g., 'John is a good student') or part of modal-like constructions with 'have' (e.g., 'John has to study'). Don’t assume 'be' + another word automatically signals the passive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myth: passive always avoids first person
rubrics_metrics.description: Passive voice can occur in first person; presence of 'I' or 'we' does not guarantee active voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'I was hit by the dodgeball.' Evaluate voice by structure (actor's grammatical position), not by presence/absence of first person pronouns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myth: never use the passive
rubrics_metrics.description: You should not dogmatically ban passive voice; there are legitimate contexts where passive is preferable or acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The handout lists specific cases where passive is useful (emphasizing an object, de-emphasizing an unknown subject, when readers don't need to know the actor). Make informed choices about when passive serves your rhetorical goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myth: rely on grammar checkers to find passive
rubrics_metrics.description: Grammar checkers catch only a fraction of passive-voice usage and are not reliable for identifying all passive constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not depend solely on automated tools — learn to identify passive using the formula and evaluate sentences yourself during revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and meaning: specify the actor; prefer active for precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructors often prefer active constructions because passive sentences frequently lack explicit reference to the actor, making meaning ambiguous or imprecise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When passive hides who did the action, convert to active to clarify (e.g., 'A new system of drug control laws was set up.' → 'The Lao People’s Revolutionary Party set up a new system of drug control laws.'). Ensure thesis statements are especially clear and avoid passive there if it obscures meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid passive as a crutch in summarizing plots/history
rubrics_metrics.description: Using passive to summarize events or arguments (e.g., 'The working class was marginalized.') can signal lazy or imprecise thinking and deprive the reader of causal/contextual detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer active constructions that connect actors, systems, and causes. Avoid vague, decontextualized passive summaries; instead identify agents and mechanisms to show rigorous understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific writing — lab reports: possible preference for passive in Methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Some instructors or journals prefer passive voice in lab reports/Materials and Methods to create an objective tone and to remove the writer from the description of procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check instructor/journal preference. Note growing acceptance of first-person active (e.g., 'we sequenced the human genome'). Even in lab reports, you can often use active verbs (support, indicate, suggest, yield, show) in other sections. Use passive when it better serves the objective tone in Methods, but be flexible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific writing — literature/review: attribute claims to researchers (use active)
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting what other scientists have done or concluded, active constructions that identify actors (e.g., 'Researchers have concluded') clarify the source of claims more than impersonal passive statements ('Heart disease is considered the leading cause of death').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer phrasing that attributes conclusions or findings to researchers or studies to make relationships and evidence clearer. Examples: 'Research points to...' or 'Researchers have concluded that...'

rubrics_metrics.name: Political/ethical use: passive can obscure responsibility (avoid when hiding blame)
rubrics_metrics.description: Passive constructions are sometimes used to hide blame or obscure who is responsible for actions (Orwell's 'swindles and perversions').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be critically aware of this usage in others and avoid passive when it would shield actors from accountability (e.g., 'Mistakes were made.'). Explicitly name responsible parties when responsibility matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: When passive is appropriate — emphasize the object
rubrics_metrics.description: Use passive when you want to emphasize the object or patient of an action rather than the actor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'One hundred votes are required to pass the bill.' The passive places emphasis on the number of votes required rather than the bill; an active phrasing would shift emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: When passive is appropriate — de-emphasize unknown subject/actor
rubrics_metrics.description: If the actor is unknown or irrelevant, passive can be useful to avoid inventing or misattributing an agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Over 120 different contaminants have been dumped into the river.' If you truly don't know who dumped them, passive is acceptable. If you do know, prefer naming the actor for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: When passive is appropriate — readers don't need to know the actor
rubrics_metrics.description: Use passive when the intended audience cares more about the object/event than the actor (e.g., birth announcements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare contexts: a family announcement ('Baby Sophia was delivered at 3:30 a.m.') may appropriately omit the doctor, while a hospital report should include the actor. Anticipate reader expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify (revision checklist for spotting passive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Step-by-step detection strategy to find passive constructions in your writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for 'to be' + past participle; ask if the sentence describes an action and whether the actor is at the front or missing; check for an ending 'by...' phrase though 'by' alone isn't conclusive. If you don't see both components, it's likely not passive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate (questions to decide whether to keep passive)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of evaluative questions to determine whether passive is appropriate in each instance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: Is the doer/actor indicated? Should you indicate him/her/it/them? Does it matter who’s responsible? Would your reader ask you to clarify? Do you use passive in your thesis statement? Are you using passive as a crutch in summaries? Do you intend to emphasize the object?

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise (how to convert passive to active)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical revision strategy to change passive sentences to active ones by restoring the actor to subject position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Switch word order to make the actor the grammatical subject and put it before the verb. Examples: 'The metropolis has been scorched by the dragon’s fiery breath.' → 'The dragon has scorched the metropolis.' 'When her house was invaded, Penelope had to think...' → 'After suitors invaded her house, Penelope had to think...'. Use this as a default revision move when clarity requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision mindset: draft now, revise for voice later
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice about process: don't let fear of passive inhibit drafting; focus on detecting and revising passive during revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity often emerges in revision rather than the first draft. Make active choices about voice when revising. There is nothing grammatically wrong with passive; the goal is to 'recognize when you should, when you shouldn’t, and when your instructor just doesn’t want you to.'
